records.label: Large consanguineous ARID family

variants.as_reported: non-synonymous sequence change in the SWIP gene

quotes: In a large consanguineous family with autosomal recessive intellectual disability (ARID), we have combined homozygosity mapping, targeted exon enrichment and high-throughput sequencing to identify the underlying gene defect.
including a non-synonymous sequence change in the SWIP [Strumpellin and WASH (Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein and scar homolog)-interacting protein] gene
this gene defect was considered as causative for ID in this family.

records.label: Younger sister (aged 4 years)

phenotypes.text: congenital absence of the right internal carotid artery

records.segregation: each variant inherited from one parent
quotes: Two sisters, aged 4 and 5.5 years, had a stop-gain and a missense variants, each inherited from one parent (p.(Gln442*) and p.(Asp1048Gly)).
Both had learning disabilities, macrocephaly, dysmorphic features, skeletal anomalies, and subependymal heterotopic nodules.
In addition, the younger sibling had a congenital absence of the right internal carotid and bilateral sensorineural hearing loss.

records.label: Third patient (aged 34 years)
records.segregation: one variant inherited from each parent
quotes: The third patient was aged 34 years and had two missense variants, one inherited from each parent (p.(Lys1079Arg) and p.(His503Arg)).
This patient presented with mild ID, short stature, and microcephaly.

records.label: Seven children with homozygous WASHC4 c.3056C>G
records.age_last: now an average of 21 years old
quotes: We retrospectively analyzed clinical findings from seven children with homozygous WASHC4c.3056C>G mutations (obtained by Dr. Rajab in 2010 at the Royal Hospital, Muscat, Oman). The original report of these human subjects and parental consent for data use can be found in Ropers et al., 2011.
While developmental delay or learning difficulties were the primary impetus for medical evaluation, all patients also exhibited motor symptoms (mean age=10.4 years old, Figure 8H).
The patients’ movements were described as ‘clumsy’ with notable fine motor difficulties, dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, and mild dysarthria on clinical exam (Figure 8H).

records.label: Two sisters with homozygous WASHC4 variant
quotes: Homozygous WASHC4 variant in two sisters causes a syndromic phenotype defined by dysmorphisms, intellectual disability, profound developmental disorder, and skeletal muscle involvement.
Here, we report two siblings with a homozygous WASHC4 variant expanding the clinical spectrum of the disease

notes.statement: Gangfuß et al. (2022) found that proteomic profiling of fibroblasts from a WASHC4-deficient patient showed dysregulation of proteins relevant to maintaining the neuromuscular axis. Immunostaining of the same patient's muscle biopsy confirmed dysregulation of proteins needed for proper muscle function.
quotes: Proteomic profiling of fibroblasts of the WASHC4-deficient patient revealed dysregulation of proteins relevant for the maintenance of the neuromuscular axis.
Immunostaining on a muscle biopsy derived from the same patient confirmed dysregulation of proteins relevant for proper muscle function

notes.statement: Gangfuß et al. (2022) reported that histologic and coherent anti-Stokes Raman scattering microscopy studies supported a functional role for WASHC4 in humans in protein processing and clearance. They stated that their findings showed skeletal muscle involvement in patients for the first time.
quotes: The results of histological and coherent anti-Stokes Raman scattering microscopic studies support the concept of a functional role of the WASHC4 protein in humans by altering protein processing and clearance.
highlighted, for the first time, the involvement of skeletal muscle in patients

notes.statement: Courtland et al. (2021) retrospectively re-evaluated the original reports of the human SWIPP1019R (WASHC4 c.3056C>G) patients and noted that, although developmental delay or learning difficulties prompted medical evaluation, all patients also exhibited motor symptoms; recent communication with the parents, whose children were then an average of 21 years old, revealed no notable symptom exacerbation.
quotes: While developmental delay or learning difficulties were the primary impetus for medical evaluation, all patients also exhibited motor symptoms (mean age=10.4 years old, Figure 8H).
Recent communication with the parents of these patients, who are now an average of 21 years old, revealed no notable symptom exacerbation.

notes.statement: Courtland et al. (2021) noted that an autosomal recessive mutation in WASHC4 (c.3056C>G; p.Pro1019Arg) had been identified in a cohort of children with non-syndromic intellectual disability by Ropers et al. (2011), and that cell lines derived from these patients exhibited decreased abundance of WASH proteins.
quotes: In particular, an autosomal recessive mutation in WASHC4 (c.3056C>G; p.Pro1019Arg) was identified in a cohort of children with non-syndromic intellectual disability (Ropers et al., 2011).

Cell lines derived from these patients exhibited decreased abundance of WASH proteins, leading the authors to hypothesize that the observed cognitive deficits in SWIPP1019R patients resulted from disruption of neuronal WASH signaling (Ropers et al., 2011).

notes.statement: Courtland et al. (2021) found that the P1019R substitution lies in a region of SWIP thought to be critical for binding to the WASH component Strumpellin, and showed in HEK cells that mutant SWIP co-immunoprecipitated significantly less Strumpellin and WASH1 than wild-type SWIP (54.8% and 41.4% of wild type, respectively), indicating that the mutation hinders WASH complex formation.
quotes: This C>G point mutation results in a Proline>Arginine substitution at position 1019 of SWIP’s amino acid sequence (Figure 2A), a region thought to be critical for its binding to the WASH component, Strumpellin (Jia et al., 2010; Ropers et al., 2011).

Compared to WT, MUT SWIP co-immunoprecipitated significantly less Strumpellin and WASH1 (IP: 54.8% and 41.4% of WT SWIP, respectively), suggesting that the SWIPP1019R mutation hinders WASH complex formation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

notes.statement: Courtland et al. (2021) generated a mouse model of the human WASHC4 c.3056C>G mutation by CRISPR introduction of a CCT>CGT point mutation into exon 29 of murine Washc4, and found that whole-brain lysate of homozygous mutant mice showed markedly decreased abundance of the WASH complex members Strumpellin (3.8% of wild type) and WASH1 (1.1% of wild type), phenocopying data from the human patients.
quotes: A CRISPR-induced CCT>CGT point mutation was introduced into exon 29 of Washc4.
Strumpellin (WT 100.0±5.1%, MUT 3.8±0.9%, t2.14=18.60, p=0.0021) and WASH1 (WT 100.0±4.3%, MUT 1.1±0.4%, t2.1=22.77, p=0.0018) were significantly decreased.
These results phenocopied data from the human patients (Ropers et al., 2011) and suggested that the WASH complex is unstable in the presence of this SWIP point mutation in vivo.

notes.statement: Using quantitative spatial proteomics of SWIPP1019R mouse brain, Courtland et al. (2021) found that 23 of 49 protein covariation modules differed between wild-type and mutant brain, with the WASH/endosomal module M38 significantly decreased and a lysosomal module M36 (containing cathepsins, hydrolases such as HEXA, GBA, GLB1, MAN2B1, MAN2B2, and progranulin) significantly increased in mutant brain.
quotes: Twenty-three of the 49 modules exhibited significant differences in WT versus MUT brain (Bonferroni p-adjust < 0.05; Supplementary file 3; Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995; Hochberg, 1988).

Across all fractions, the abundance of M38 was significantly lower in MUT brain compared to WT, providing evidence that the SWIPP1019R mutation reduces the stability of this protein subnetwork and impairs its function (Figure 3C).
In contrast to the decreased abundance of the WASH complex/endosome module (M38), M36 exhibited increased abundance in MUT brain (Figure 4C).

notes.statement: Courtland et al. (2021) found that cultured cortical neurons from SWIPP1019R mutant mice had larger somatic EEA1-positive early endosomal puncta than wild-type neurons with no change in puncta number, and fewer but larger Cathepsin D-positive lysosomal puncta, supporting morphologic abnormalities of the endo-lysosomal pathway.
quotes: (G) Graph of the average EEA1+ volume size per soma shows larger EEA1+ volumes in MUT neurons (WT 0.15±0.01 µm3, n=24 neurons; MUT 0.30±0.02 µm3, n=24 neurons; U=50, p<0.0001).
Conversely, MUT neurons exhibited significantly less Cathepsin D+ puncta than WT neurons (Figure 5H), but the remaining puncta were significantly larger than those of WT neurons (Figure 5I and K).

notes.statement: Courtland et al. (2021) found that 10-month-old SWIPP1019R mutant mice had significantly increased cleaved caspase-3 staining selectively in motor cortex (44.01% vs 25.38% of nuclei) but not at adolescence, and that electron microscopy of 7-month-old mutant motor cortex showed increased size and number of electron-dense lipofuscin deposits, indicators of neurodegeneration.
quotes: No difference is seen at P42, but the amount of CC3+ nuclei is significantly higher in aged MUT mice (P42 WT 6.97 ± 0.80%, P42 MUT 5.26 ± 0.90%, 10mo WT 25.38 ± 2.05%, 10mo MUT 44.01 ± 1.90%, H=74.12, p<0.0001).
Strikingly, we observed large electron-dense inclusions in the cell bodies of MUT neurons (arrows, Figure 6L; pseudo-colored region, 6N).
(O) Graph of areas of electron-dense regions of interest (ROI) shows increased ROI size in MUT neurons (WT 2.4×105 ± 2.8×104 nm2, n=50 ROIs; MUT 8.2×105±9.7×104 nm2, n=75 ROIs; U=636, p<0.0001).

notes.statement: Courtland et al. (2021) found that SWIPP1019R mutant mice showed normal novel object recognition and Y-maze performance but a persistent deficit in cued fear memory recall at both adolescence and adulthood, with intact responses to footshock and tones, and progressive motor dysfunction with nearly 50% reduced rotarod retention at both ages and gait abnormalities (longer swing time, longer strides, reduced homologous coupling) emerging in adulthood.
quotes: Interestingly, MUT mice performed equivalently to WT mice in episodic and working memory paradigms, including novel object recognition and Y-maze alternations (Figure 7—figure supplement 1). However, in a fear conditioning task, MUT mice displayed a significant deficit in cued fear memory (Figure 7).

At both ages, the MUT mice exhibited an almost 50% reduction in their ability to remain on the rod (top, P45: WT 169.9 ± 25.7 s, MUT 83.8 ± 15.9 s, U=35, p=0.0054; bottom, 5.5mo: WT 135.9 ± 20.9 s, MUT 66.7 ± 9.5 s, t18=3.011, p=0.0075).

These findings demonstrate that SWIPP1019R results in progressive motor function decline that was detectable by the rotarod task at adolescence, but which became more prominent with age, as both gait and strength functions deteriorated.

notes.statement: Using in vivo BioID with a WASH1 (Washc1) probe expressed in mouse brain under the neuron-specific synapsin-1 promoter, Courtland et al. (2021) identified a neuronal WASH proteome of 175 significantly enriched proteins, including all five WASH complex components, 13 known WASH interactors, and proteins of endosomal, endocytic, cytoskeletal and postsynaptic function, supporting a major endosomal trafficking role for the WASH complex in brain.
quotes: The resulting neuronal WASH proteome included 175 proteins that were significantly enriched (fold-change≥4.0, Benjamini–Hochberg FDR<0.05, Figure 1G; Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995).

Of these proteins, we identified all five WASH complex components (Figure 1H), as well as 13 previously reported WASH complex interactors (Figure 1I; McNally et al., 2017; Phillips-Krawczak et al., 2015; Simonetti and Cullen, 2019; Singla et al., 2019), which provided strong validity for our proteomic approach and analyses.
Taken together, these results support a major endosomal trafficking role of the WASH complex in mouse brain.

notes.statement: Courtland et al. (2021) noted that dominant missense mutations in WASHC5 (Strumpellin) are associated with hereditary spastic paraplegia (SPG8), whereas autosomal recessive point mutations in WASHC4 (SWIP) and WASHC5 are associated with syndromic and non-syndromic intellectual disabilities.
quotes: Consistent with the association between the endosomal trafficking system and pathology, dominant missense mutations in WASHC5 (protein: Strumpellin) are associated with hereditary spastic paraplegia (SPG8) (de Bot et al., 2013; Valdmanis et al., 2007), and autosomal recessive point mutations in WASHC4 (protein: SWIP) and WASHC5 are associated with syndromic and non-syndromic intellectual disabilities (Assoum et al., 2020; Elliott et al., 2013; Ropers et al., 2011).

notes.statement: Courtland et al. (2021) concluded that their data support a mechanistic model whereby SWIPP1019R causes loss of WASH complex function, resulting in endo-lysosomal disruption and accumulation of neurodegenerative markers including unfolded protein response modulators, lysosomal enzymes, lipofuscin, and cleaved caspase-3 over time, leading to cognitive deficits and progressive motor impairments.
quotes: Taken together, the data presented here support a mechanistic model whereby SWIPP1019R causes a loss of WASH complex function, resulting in endo-lysosomal disruption and accumulation of neurodegenerative markers, such as upregulation of unfolded protein response modulators and lysosomal enzymes, as well as build-up of lipofuscin and cleaved caspase-3 over time.

notes.statement: Courtland et al. (2021) observed that although the human SWIPP1019R mutation has not been classified as a neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis, findings in their mutant mouse model, including lipofuscin accumulation, suggested that loss of WASH complex function leads to phenotypes strongly resembling the NCLs.
quotes: While the human SWIPP1019R mutation has not been classified as an NCL (Ropers et al., 2011), findings from our mutant mouse model suggest that loss of WASH complex function leads to phenotypes bearing strong resemblance to NCLs, including lipofuscin accumulation (Figures 5–8).

notes.statement: Assoum et al. (2020) concluded that KIAA1033 is responsible for a heterogeneous autosomal recessive intellectual disability phenotype and that more descriptions will be needed to refine the clinical phenotype.
quotes: We conclude that KIAA1033 is responsible for a heterogeneous ARID phenotype, and additional description will be needed to refine the clinical phenotype.

notes.statement: In a large consanguineous family with autosomal recessive intellectual disability, Ropers et al. (2011) combined homozygosity mapping, targeted exon enrichment, and high-throughput sequencing and, after SNP filtering, found only 2 remaining changes, including a nonsynonymous change in SWIP, which they considered causative based on high pathogenicity and conservation scores and functional considerations.
quotes: After appropriate single-nucleotide polymorphism filtering, only two molecular changes remained, including a non-synonymous sequence change in the SWIP
Based on high pathogenicity and evolutionary conservation scores as well as functional considerations, this gene defect was considered as causative for ID in this family.

notes.statement: Ropers et al. (2011) showed that the SWIP mutation led to significantly reduced SWIP levels and to destabilization of the entire WASH complex, which is involved in actin polymerization and endosomal transport.
quotes: we could show that this mutation leads to significantly reduced SWIP levels and to destabilization of the entire WASH complex.
a member of the recently discovered WASH complex, which is involved in actin polymerization and multiple endosomal transport processes.
